description: During the process of washing the material (Becker), the tip of the material was broken which caused a cut of the 5th finger of the right hand
sif_reason: This event involves breakage of laboratory glassware (a "Becker," likely a Beaker) during a washing task, resulting in a cut to a single finger. This is a low-energy mechanical hazard — the breaking glass produces a sharp edge that caused localized, minor trauma. While cuts can occasionally escalate to tendon, nerve, or vascular damage, the mechanism and body part involved (single finger, 5th digit) do not indicate a realistic pathway to serious injury or fatality, even under a moderately worse-case variation of this scenario.
evidence_text: "During the process of washing the material (Becker), the tip of the material was broken which caused a cut of the 5th finger of the right hand"
hazard_notes: harp/broken glass edge (low kinetic energy, contact-type hazard)
exposure_notes: direct hand contact with glass labware during a manual washing task; the glassware broke while in-hand or in-contact, exposing the finger to the fractured edge
consequence_notes: Under a worse-case variation (deeper cut, damage to tendon/nerve/blood vessel, or a larger glass fragment causing a more severe laceration), this could result in a more serious hand injury requiring surgical repair; however, life-threatening or permanently disabling outcomes are unlikely from this specific mechanism
barrier_notes: Weak/absent — no indication that cut-resistant gloves were worn during the glassware washing task, and no mention of an inspection process to identify weakened/cracked glassware before handling
boundary_selection_reason: Existing UNCERTAIN label; verify that missing information is materially decision-changing.
adjudication_reason: The missing information flagged as the basis for "UNCERTAIN" (cut depth, glove use, glass fragment size, inspection history) is not materially decision-changing. The hazard energy class here — a broken glass edge causing a laceration to a single finger during a washing task — is inherently low-energy and mechanically bounded. Even under the most severe plausible variation of this exact mechanism (deeper laceration, tendon/nerve damage, larger shard), the realistic ceiling of consequence is a serious hand injury, not a life-threatening or permanently disabling outcome. Unlike chemical, electrical, height, or heavy-machinery hazards — where missing PPE/control details can swing the assessment from "minor" to "fatal-potential" — a lab glassware cut to a finger does not have that kind of severity ceiling. Therefore the absence of PPE and depth details does not create genuine uncertainty about SIF classification; it only affects the actual injury severity, not the potential ceiling.
adjudication_notes:
Hazard/energy, exposure, and consequence pathway are clearly and completely described in the narrative — there is no ambiguity about the mechanism itself.
The only unknowns (glove use, glass fragment size, cut depth) would affect whether the actual injury was minor or moderate, not whether the event could plausibly have escalated to SIF-level severity.
No new facts, assumptions, or unsupported details were introduced in this adjudication; the original evidence, hazard, exposure, and barrier findings from the prior annotation are affirmed as accurate and sufficient.
This case is distinguishable from genuinely uncertain SIF cases (e.g., chemical splashes near the face/eyes, cuts near major arteries/tendons with unclear location, or falls with unclear height) where missing information does change the plausible severity ceiling.

evidence_text: the sleeve of the employee's coat had contact with nitric acid, absorbing a small amount that came to reach the left forearm, causing a 1st degree burn
hazard_notes: Chemical energy — corrosive/oxidizing hazardous substance (nitric acid), a Class A hazard capable of severe tissue damage
exposure_notes: Direct skin contact via clothing absorption; sleeve of PPE (coat) absorbed acid, which then reached the left forearm — indicates a control (PPE) was present but was breached or insufficient (permeable/absorbent fabric, no chemical-resistant sleeve or apron)
consequence_notes: Under marginally different conditions (higher concentration, larger volume, longer contact time before wash-off, contact with face/eyes, or delayed recognition since the acid soaked through fabric before reaching skin) this could result in severe chemical burns, permanent scarring, or greater bodily harm — meeting SIF severity criteria
barrier_notes: Weak/failed barrier — the coat (likely standard lab coat, not chemical-resistant) did not prevent acid penetration to skin. This represents a failed or absent engineering/PPE control for the energy level involved
boundary_selection_reason: Existing UNCERTAIN label; verify that missing information is materially decision-changing.
adjudication_reason: Applying the adjudication constraint "I did not invent unsupported material changes," the prior reasoning elevated this case by hypothesizing exposure routes not present in the narrative — specifically "contact with eyes," "inhalation of fumes," "larger splash," and "delayed recognition." None of these are evidenced. The narrative states a small amount of nitric acid was absorbed through the coat sleeve, reaching the left forearm, and resulted in a 1st degree burn — the mildest clinical burn classification (superficial, affecting only the outer skin layer, typically healing without scarring). This is a materially different fact pattern than a case involving the face, eyes, or airway. Substituting a higher-severity outcome (severe burns, permanent scarring, deep tissue damage) to justify SIF-potential requires assuming a different quantity, concentration, or body location than what is documented — precisely the kind of invented material change the adjudication rule excludes. Assessed strictly on the stated hazard/exposure/consequence, this is a small-quantity, non-critical-location, low-severity chemical exposure.
adjudication_notes:
Hazard/energy: nitric acid is genuinely a strong oxidizing/corrosive acid — correctly identified and not in question.
Exposure: confirmed as limited — a small amount, absorbed through clothing, contacting the forearm (skin location with no proximity to eyes, airway, or mucous membranes).
Consequence: the actual and only evidenced consequence is a 1st degree (superficial) burn — the narrative does not support escalation to "severe chemical burns," "permanent injury," or "life-threatening harm" without inventing a different exposure scenario.
Barrier: the coat sleeve did absorb acid rather than fully blocking it, which is a legitimate PPE-adequacy gap worth corrective action (e.g., chemical-resistant sleeves for nitric acid handling) — but a control gap alone, without an evidenced high-severity outcome or exposure route, does not meet SIF criteria.
This is consistent with the corrected adjudications for industrial_safety_000250 and industrial_safety_000346: in all three chemical cases, the original "Potential SIF" classifications relied on hypothesized worse-case exposure routes (eyes, inhalation, larger volume) rather than the exposure and consequence actually documented

The fact that this was described as only "a drop" is what kept the actual outcome minor; the potential consequence given the hazard energy and proximity to sensitive areas is high.

description: Once the painting of the pumping pipe has been completed, the person involved involuntarily touches his face, with his hand (with gloves) full of paint, and to clean himself he makes use of a dry industrial cloth and begins to rub his face, for a period of time from 30 to 40 seconds continuously, until finally the paint on the face is cleaned, this friction generates the described injury.
sif_reason: The actual injury mechanism here is friction/abrasion from prolonged rubbing with a dry industrial cloth, not the paint chemical itself. While paint exposure to skin/face is undesirable and the cleaning method used was poor practice, this event does not involve a high-energy hazard (no corrosive/toxic chemical injury, no eye contact mentioned, no respiratory exposure). The consequence — skin irritation/abrasion from friction — has low potential to escalate to serious injury or fatality, even under a worse-case variation of the same scenario.

exposure_notes: Direct, prolonged (30–40 seconds) friction/rubbing contact between a dry industrial cloth and facial skin, following inadvertent hand-to-face contact with wet paint
consequence_notes: : Localized skin abrasion, irritation, or redness from friction; if paint contained irritating/toxic solvents and contact had involved the eyes or mucous membranes instead of general facial skin, the potential consequence could have been more serious (chemical eye injury) — but as described, the realistic escalation potential remains low to moderate, not SIF-level
barrier_notes: improper cleaning method used (dry friction instead of appropriate solvent/water-based cleaning or eyewash-type response for facial chemical contact); indicates gaps in training/procedure for skin decontamination after chemical (paint) contact, and glove use did not prevent hand-to-face transfer
boundary_selection_reason: Chemical case whose reasoning may rely on changed concentration/quantity/contact assumptions.
adjudication_reason: The boundary reason correctly flags this as a case where a "YES" determination may have relied on an unsupported counterfactual — i.e., assuming the paint was a toxic/solvent-based product, or assuming contact reached the eyes/mucous membranes, neither of which is stated in the narrative. Applying the adjudication constraint "I did not invent unsupported material changes," the assessment must be grounded in what actually occurred: hand-to-face contact with paint (chemical contact only, no injury reported from this), followed by 30–40 seconds of dry-cloth friction (the actual stated injury mechanism). The described injury arose from mechanical friction/abrasion, not chemical burn, toxic absorption, or ocular exposure. A prior YES label appears to have weighted the chemical hazard (paint) and its worst-case potential (toxic solvent, eye contact) rather than the actual documented exposure and consequence pathway. Correcting for that, the realistic severity ceiling of this specific, described event — friction abrasion from cleaning paint off facial skin — does not meet SIF criteria.
adjudication_notes:
Hazard/energy: the narrative supports friction (mechanical) as the actual injury-causing energy; paint chemical exposure is present but not established as the injury mechanism (no burn, no irritation-from-chemical noted).
Exposure: confirmed as prolonged dry friction contact with skin; no evidence of eye, mucous membrane, or inhalation exposure to substantiate a chemical-injury severity pathway.
Consequence: as documented, consistent with localized abrasion/irritation — a real but bounded outcome.
Barrier: poor decontamination procedure (dry cloth instead of proper cleaning agent) is a legitimate control gap and worth corrective action, but a control gap alone does not elevate SIF potential without a plausible high-severity exposure pathway actually present in the narrative.
This is distinguished from cases like industrial_safety_000250 (sulfuric acid to the upper lip) or industrial_safety_000190 (ammonia splash to the face), where the stated exposure itself (corrosive/toxic chemical directly contacting skin/face) carries an inherent high-severity ceiling. Here, the stated exposure to paint did not itself produce the injury — friction did.

description: When performing the Doosan RB-10 equipment hammer repair, the employee tries to remove the suspenders with the support of a 25-pound rope; At the moment of receiving the blow the brace or bolt causes a splinter to be released, expelling and impacting on the lower left limb causing metal embedding in it. The collaborator did not notice immediately.
sif_reason: The repair involved striking/removing a mechanical component under tension or restraint. The impact caused a metal fragment to be projected into the worker's lower limb, demonstrating uncontrolled stored/mechanical energy and projectile potential. A similar release directed toward the head, eyes, or torso could cause life-altering or fatal injury.
evidence_text: During repair of the Doosan RB-10 hammer, the employee attempted to remove the suspenders using a 25-pound rope. When the component was struck, the brace/bolt released a metal splinter that was projected into the lower left limb, becoming embedded.
hazard_notes: Stored mechanical energy and projectile energy from the brace/bolt during removal and impact.
exposure_notes: The employee was in close proximity to the component and in the potential line of fire while striking/removing it.
consequence_notes: Fatality or life-altering injury, including penetrating trauma, severe laceration, eye injury, or potentially fatal injury if a metal fragment were projected toward a vital body area.
barrier_notes: Line-of-fire, restraint, and controlled disassembly barriers were inadequate or ineffective. The component was struck while the worker remained exposed to potential projectile release. Appropriate restraint, controlled removal methods, exclusion zones, and suitable PPE should prevent personnel exposure.
boundary_selection_reason: High-energy exposure with an explicit protective barrier that may affect the SIF decision.
adjudication_reason: The repair involved stored mechanical energy and uncontrolled projectile release. A metal splinter was ejected when the brace/bolt was struck and became embedded in the worker's leg. This mechanism could credibly cause serious or fatal injury if the projectile struck a vital body area.
adjudication_notes: The worker was in the line of fire during removal of the component. The actual event demonstrates that the restraint/disassembly method did not fully control the stored energy. The fact that the fragment struck the lower limb rather than a vital area does not eliminate the SIF potential of the mechanism.

description: When performing shotcrete casting for resane on Cruise 791 Nv. 1940 at 02:50 p.m. approximately, the operator was placed on the left side of the equipment and started the release of 02 cubic meters, at that time decided to paralyze the task for a few minutes due to a leak of water in the roof box that did not allow the adhesion of the shotcrete to the rock (setting). When restarting the shotcrete launch the operator that was on the left side moved to the right side of the equipment, while the assistant and the operator mixkret to see that there was no pumping went to verify what happened and when they returned they realized that the operator was not, so they assume that he had fallen down the chimney, they left the job to ask for help immediately. The emergency response brigade and the medical service are activated, who verify the death of the collaborator. The accident investigation begins.
sif_reason: The operator fell down a chimney/vertical opening while performing underground shotcrete work and died. A fall into a vertical excavation or shaft presents an immediate and credible fatality mechanism.
evidence_text: During shotcrete application at Cruise 791, Nv. 1940, the operator moved from one side of the equipment to the other. When the crew returned, he was missing and was presumed to have fallen down the chimney. The emergency brigade and medical service responded and confirmed the collaborator's death.
hazard_notes: Gravity / fall-from-height energy associated with an unprotected or inadequately controlled vertical chimney/opening.
exposure_notes: The operator was working and moving adjacent to the chimney/vertical opening during the shotcrete activity.
consequence_notes: Fatality or life-altering injury from a fall into the vertical opening, including fatal traumatic injury. Fatality actually occurred in this event.
barrier_notes: Fall-prevention and access-control barriers were inadequate or ineffective. The vertical opening was apparently accessible to the operator without sufficient protection to prevent a fall. Guarding/barricading, physical covers, controlled access, fall protection where required, and verification of the work area should have prevented the exposure.
boundary_selection_reason: High-energy exposure with an explicit protective barrier that may affect the SIF decision.
adjudication_reason: The event involved a fall into a vertical chimney/opening, resulting in the worker's death. This is an unequivocal credible fatality mechanism and meets the SIF potential boundary.
adjudication_notes: The operator was working in the vicinity of the vertical opening and subsequently disappeared, with the crew assuming he had fallen down the chimney. Emergency responders confirmed his death. The narrative supports direct exposure to a fatal fall hazard. The presence or effectiveness of other controls does not remove the SIF potential because the described barrier did not prevent the fatal exposure.
